uncited: IBGS decomposes the final pixel color into a base color rendered via standard 3DGS volume rendering and a learned residual derived from multi-view features.
The method involves feature extraction from source views, residual prediction via a convolutional decoder, and optional exposure correction.
*   3D Gaussian primitives (centers $\mu_i$, covariances $\Sigma_i$, opacities $o_i$, spherical harmonics coefficients $h_i$, and normal vectors $n_i$).
*   Camera poses and intrinsics for the target view and $M$ neighboring source views.
*   **Time Complexity:** Dominated by the standard 3DGS rasterization and the lightweight 9-layer CNN decoder.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Storage footprint is identical to standard 3DGS (Gaussians + SH coefficients).
Performance depends on the quality of multi-view correspondences.
*   **When to use:** When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required, especially for scenes with complex lighting or fine textures, and storage is constrained.
*   **When not to use:** If source views are not available or have poor overlap/visibility with the target view.
IBGS was proposed by Hoang Chuong Nguyen, Wei Mao, Jose M. Alvarez, and Miaomiao Liu from the Australian National University and NVIDIA.

The method addresses the limitations of 3DGS, which uses low-degree spherical harmonics to model view-dependent color, limiting its ability to capture spatially varying color and effects like specular highlights.

IBGS leverages image-based rendering principles to "borrow" pixels from source views, modeling the residual color to supplement the base 3DGS rendering [S1].

The claim states that IBGS leverages image-based rendering principles to 'borrow' pixels from source views and models a residual color to supplement the base 3DGS rendering. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this: 1) The abstract states IBGS 'models each pixel color as a combination of a base color from standard 3DGS rendering and a learned residual inferred from neighboring training images.' 2) The introduction mentions that 'Image-based rendering aims to generate novel views by “borrowing” pixels from a set of source images,' and the method projects intersection points onto neighboring training images to obtain pixel colors (warped colors) which are used to predict the residual. 3) The mathematical formulation shows the final color is the sum of the base color $c(p)$ and the residual predicted by network $F$ using features from source views. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

*   **Gaussian Attributes:** Each Gaussian $i$ stores center $\mu_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, covariance $\Sigma_i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$, opacity $o_i \in \mathbb{R}$, SH coefficients $h_i$ (degree $l=2$), and normal vector $n_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ [S1].

The claim lists five specific attributes for each Gaussian: center ($mu_i$), covariance ($Sigma_i$), opacity ($o_i$), SH coefficients ($h_i$), and normal vector ($n_i$). The evidence supports all these points: 1) The center $mu_i$ is mentioned in the intersection point formula (Eq. 3) as part of the plane parameterization. 2) The opacity $o_i$ is explicitly defined in the notes regarding the base color calculation ($alpha_i = o_i G_{2D}^i(p)$). 3) The SH coefficients $h_i$ are explicitly listed in the notes and used in the base color formula ($c_i = Psi_l(h_i, v_i)$). 4) The normal vector $n_i$ is explicitly stated in the notes ('incorporate a normal vector n_i') and used in Eq. 3. 5) While the covariance $Sigma_i$ is not explicitly named in the provided text snippets, it is a fundamental component of the Gaussian distribution $G_{2D}^i(p)$ referenced in the opacity formula ($alpha_i = o_i G_{2D}^i(p)$) and is standard in 3DGS. Since the claim states that these are the attributes stored, and the evidence confirms the presence of these specific variables in the mathematical formulation of the method described, the claim is supported.
